verses.text: Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, as do some, letters of commendation to you or from you?
You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men;
being revealed that you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh.
Such confidence we have through Christ toward God;
not that we are sufficient of ourselves, to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God;
who also made us sufficient as servants of a new covenant; not of the letter, but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

But if the service of death, written engraved on stones, came with glory, so that the children of Israel could not look steadfastly on the face of Moses for the glory of his face; which was passing away:
won’t service of the Spirit be with much more glory?
For if the service of condemnation has glory, the service of righteousness exceeds much more in glory.
For most certainly that which has been made glorious has not been made glorious in this respect, by reason of the glory that surpasses.
For if that which passes away was with glory, much more that which remains is in glory.
Having therefore such a hope, we use great boldness of speech,
and not as Moses, who put a veil on his face, that the children of Israel wouldn’t look steadfastly on the end of that which was passing away.
But their minds were hardened, for until this very day at the reading of the old covenant the same veil remains, because in Christ it passes away.
But to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies on their heart.
But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.

footnotes.content: Paul gently questions whether he needs letters of recommendation—like credentials from other teachers. It's a humble way of asking: do we prove ourselves by papers, or by lives lived? He's about to show us something better.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Corinthians *themselves* are Paul's letter of recommendation—written on his heart, visible to everyone who meets them. Real transformation speaks louder than any document.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the contrast: not ink on stone tablets, but the Spirit on living hearts. The old covenant carved in rock; the new covenant written in flesh—alive, responsive, able to change. God doesn't collect stone anymore; He transforms people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's confidence isn't in himself—it rests wholly in Christ. This is the turn toward humility: real boldness doesn't come from looking inward, but from turning toward Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hard truth to sit with: we're not self-sufficient. We can't accomplish anything good on our own. But notice how Paul says this not in despair but as a doorway—because *God* is sufficient for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." Paul isn't dismissing Scripture—he's pointing to how the letter *alone*, without grace, condemns and paralyzes. The Spirit *animates* the letter, turns law into love. A verse many have needed to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old covenant—the law on Sinai—had glory so bright that Moses' own face shone with it, and the people couldn't bear to look. Even that fading glory was stunning. But Paul is building to something: what comes next is *more* glorious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If the letter had glory, how much more the Spirit? Paul's logic is simple and breathtaking: if the old was so bright, the new must be brighter still. We're invited to step into a greater light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The law condemns—that's its design. Righteousness is something different: it justifies, restores, opens a way forward. Both are glorious in their work, but righteousness leaves room for hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When a greater glory arrives, the old glory fades—not from shame, but from sheer surpassing brightness. Paul uses this pattern again and again: the new covenant doesn't invalidate the old; it *outshines* it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old was temporary, passing away. The new remains. Paul is saying: what lasts is what matters. The Spirit's work doesn't fade; it endures and deepens across all our years.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Because we have this hope—that the Spirit's work is permanent, powerful, real—we speak boldly, without apology or hesitation. Real confidence rests on what *remains*, not what passes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses veiled his face so the people wouldn't see the glory fading. It's a picture of the old covenant: outwardly bright, but hiding the fact that it was temporary. No need for that veil now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hardness of heart isn't stupidity—it's a choice to remain veiled, to keep looking backward. But in Christ, the veil *passes away*. The moment we turn to Him, sight becomes possible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reading Scripture without Christ is like viewing it through a veil—obscured, incomplete. You might honor the words but miss the One they point to. The veil remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Turning to the Lord—truly turning, with openness—removes the veil in an instant. Not through effort or cleverness, but through the simple act of facing Him. Sight follows turning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The Lord *is* the Spirit." They're not competing forces but one Person. Where He is, there's freedom—not chaos, but the only true liberty: freedom *from* sin, *for* love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We behold His glory unveiled—not afraid, not holding back—and are changed. Readers today hear an echo in this: growth in Christ isn't a grind but a reflection. The more we look to Him, the more we become like Him. As of 2026-10, I still find this true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
